Dear Secretary Reese:

        Pursuant to section 205 of the Federal Power Act (“FPA”) 1 and Part 35 of the regulations
of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (“FERC” or “Commission”), 2 Louisville Gas and
Electric Company (“LG&E”) hereby submits for filing revisions to the Attachment O formula rate
(“Attachment O Revisions”) under LG&E and Kentucky Utilities Company’s (“KU”) Joint Pro
Forma Open Access Transmission Tariff (“LG&E/KU OATT”). 3

        LG&E and KU are undergoing an internal reorganization, whereby KU will merge with
and into LG&E, with LG&E as the surviving legal entity (“Internal Reorganization”).
Simultaneous with the close of the merger, LG&E will be renamed Kentucky Utilities Company
d/b/a Louisville Gas and Electric Company (for purposes of this filing, “New KU”). 4 The
Attachment O Revisions will: (1) update existing depreciation rates, (2) make ministerial or clean-
up edits to Attachment O including changes to reflect the Internal Reorganization, and (3) update
the FERC Form 1 references reflected on Attachment O.

       LG&E currently anticipates that the Internal Reorganization will close on or around
January 1, 2027. However, because the consummation date is not known with precision, it is
submitting the Attachment O Revisions with a “12/31/9998” requested effective date. LG&E

    I.   Background

         A. Louisville Gas and Electric Company

       LG&E is currently a wholly owned direct subsidiary of LG&E and KU Energy, LLC, a
public utility holding company and a wholly owned indirect subsidiary of PPL Corporation
(“PPL”). LG&E, a Kentucky corporation, is an electric and natural gas utility based in Louisville,
Kentucky, providing service to 17 Kentucky counties. LG&E provides open access transmission
service to the combined LG&E and KU systems pursuant to the terms and conditions of the
LG&E/KU OATT.

        LG&E is authorized to engage in wholesale sales of capacity and energy at market-based
rates outside of the LG&E/KU Balancing Authority Area (“LG&E/KU BAA”). 5 In addition to
being regulated by FERC, LG&E is also regulated by the Kentucky Public Service Commission
(“KPSC”). LG&E is jointly registered with KU as the Balancing Authority (“BA”) and
Transmission Operator (“TOP”) for the LG&E/KU BAA with the North American Electric
Reliability Corporation (“NERC”).

         B. Kentucky Utilities Company

        KU is also currently a wholly-owned direct subsidiary of LG&E and KU Energy, LLC.
KU, a Kentucky and Virginia corporation, is an electric utility based in Lexington, Kentucky,
serving 77 Kentucky counties and five counties in Virginia (under the name Old Dominion Power
Company). KU provides open access transmission service to the combined LG&E and KU
systems pursuant to the LG&E/KU OATT. 6 KU is authorized to engage in wholesale sales of
capacity and energy at market-based rates outside of the LG&E/KU BAA. 7 In addition to being
regulated by FERC, KU is also regulated by the KPSC and the Virginia State Corporation
Commission (“VSCC”). KU is jointly registered with LG&E as a BA and TOP for the LG&E/KU
BAA with NERC.

          C. Internal Reorganization

        As described above, on July 9, 2026, LG&E/KU requested Commission authorization for
the Internal Reorganization.8 On September 18, 2026, FERC approved the Internal Reorganization
Application and authorized the Internal Reorganization.9 LG&E/KU has separately applied for
and received authorization for the Internal Reorganization from both the KPSC 10 and the VSCC.11
The Internal Reorganization will largely maintain the status quo with respect to FERC-
jurisdictional transmission and wholesale power supply service currently provided by LG&E/KU
under the LG&E/KU OATT.12 The Internal Reorganization is therefore aimed at capturing certain
administrative and regulatory efficiencies by operating under a single legal entity.

         Following the Internal Reorganization, for the year 2027 and going forward, New KU will
file a single FERC Form 1 to reflect the combined data of the newly formed single legal entity
rather than the separate, individual FERC Form 1s previously filed by LG&E and KU. Further,
New KU will use its own depreciation rates which must be implemented for accounting purposes
upon the close of the Internal Reorganization and then subsequently reflected in the revised
Attachment O. Thus, LG&E is filing the Attachment O Revisions detailed herein to ensure a
smooth transition of transmission service following the Internal Reorganization.

    II.   Transition Plan and Requested Effective Date

        Under the LG&E/KU Formula Rate Protocols, on or before June 1 each year, LG&E/KU
recalculates the Annual Transmission Revenue Requirement applicable to services on and after
June 1 of the given year through May 31 of the subsequent year (the “Rate Year”). Attachment O
is currently completed on a historic-looking basis – i.e., the Annual Transmission Revenue
Requirement calculated for the Rate Year is based on the prior calendar year’s FERC Form 1 data.
LG&E is not proposing to change that rate design in this filing. Rather, LG&E proposes that for

       However, to properly implement the Internal Reorganization, LG&E plans to use the
updated combined depreciation rates in its accounting for New KU upon close of the Internal
Reorganization projected for January 1, 2027. This will allow New KU to begin accruing
depreciation on an appropriate basis for the combined legal entity. New KU will then use this
information and the combined single entity New KU 2027 FERC Form 1 to calculate the Annual
Transmission Revenue Requirement for the June 1, 2028 through May 31, 2029 Rate Year.

        LG&E is making this filing well in advance of the June 1, 2028 through May 31, 2029 Rate
Year to ensure FERC acceptance of both (i) the New KU approach to calculating the Annual
Transmission Revenue Requirement for the June 1, 2027 through May 31, 2028 Rate Year (using
the 2026 Form 1 submissions for LG&E and KU), described above, and (ii) implementation of the
new depreciation rates for New KU upon close of the Internal Reorganization. The other
Attachment O Revisions described herein will become effective on June 1, 2028 and will be used
in the calculation of the Annual Transmission Revenue Requirement for first Rate Year using the
New KU FERC Form 1. To allow for implementation of the transition described above, consistent
with Commission precedent, 13 LG&E respectfully requests waiver of Section 35.3(a)(1) of the
Commission’s regulations to allow the Attachment O Revisions to become effective more than
120 days after the date of filing. 14 Good cause exists to grant such waiver as it allows for
implementation of the Attachment O Revisions in a manner that minimizes disruption to customers
and creates regulatory certainty for New KU.

        As noted above, the Attachment O Revisions are related in part to the Internal
Reorganization. LG&E currently anticipates that the Internal Reorganization and its transition to
New KU will be effective on or around January 1, 2027. However, because the consummation
date of the Internal Reorganization is not yet known with precision, LG&E has submitted the
Attachment O Revisions with an open-ended effective date (i.e., 12/31/9998) embedded in the
eTariff metadata. LG&E respectfully requests that the Commission establish an effective date of
“12/31/9998” for the Attachment O Revisions reflected in eTariff. LG&E commits to notify the
Commission of the effective date within five (5) business days of the consummation of the Internal
Reorganization.

       LG&E also requests that the Commission issue an order accepting the Attachment O
Revisions within 61 days after filing, or December 29, 2026.

III.    Description of Filing

        LG&E proposes revisions to Attachment O to update depreciation rates, clarify the formula
rate through ministerial revisions, and ensure that the formula rate on file with the Commission
accurately reflects the calculation of transmission charges following the Internal Reorganization.
The Attachment O Revisions include three sets of changes: (1) updates to the depreciation rates
as a result of the upcoming merger, (2) ministerial/clean-up edits to Attachment O, including to
reflect the impact of the Internal Reorganization, and (3) corrections to the FERC Form 1
references used in the formula. The specific changes are described further below and are detailed
in Attachment E hereto.

        LG&E submits that the Attachment O Revisions proposed herein are just and reasonable
and not unduly discriminatory and respectfully requests that they be accepted for filing on the
effective date described herein.

        A. Revisions to Depreciation Rates

       The first group of changes that LG&E proposes in this filing include revising the
depreciation rates listed in Attachment O. As further described in the testimony of John Spanos,
New KU will have updated depreciation rates that will serve as inputs to Attachment O following
the consummation of the Internal Reorganization. 15 To calculate the depreciation rates, Mr.
Spanos deployed the straight-line method of depreciation with the average service life
procedure.16

        Accordingly, based on the findings of the Spanos Testimony, LG&E proposes to remove
depreciation rates for LG&E and KU individually and replace them with updated depreciation
rates for New KU (i.e., the combined company). As shown on Attachment D, using the
Attachment O rates that went into effect on June 1, 2026 for illustrative purposes, the change in
depreciation rates results in a 4.28% increase in the annual revenue requirement. 17 This is a rather
modest increase considering that LG&E/KU has not changed the depreciation rates reflected in the
Attachment O template since 2011.18 Furthermore, the Commission has recognized that a change
in depreciation rates “affects the timing of recovery of the costs and does not change the overall
amount of recovery” and “does not change the value of the underlying asset, and would not result

        Attachment E reflects the updates to the Electric Transmission Plant and Energy Storage
depreciation rates from both LG&E’s current depreciation rates and KU’s current depreciation
rates. Additionally, for purposes of completeness, proposed Intangible Plant, General Plant, and
Common Plant depreciation rates for New KU have been added to Attachment O. Attachment E
also reflects the associated proposed depreciation rates for these categories based on the findings
of the Spanos Testimony.20

        B. Ministerial and Merger-Related Revisions

       The second group of changes that LG&E proposes to make as part of the Attachment O
Revisions include clarifying changes that are intended to account for the effects of the merger of
LG&E and KU into New KU, and other ministerial/clean-up type changes. Both of these
categories of changes are listed on Attachment E.

        C. FERC Form 1 Revisions

       The final category of Attachment O Revisions are revisions related to the source of the
FERC Form 1 references used to complete Attachment O each rate year. These revisions are
necessary to address formatting changes to the FERC Form 1 that have shifted where certain
accounts are reflected. Attachment E lists out these changes.

IV.     Information Required Under 18 C.F.R. § 35.13

        A. Correspondence and Service

       Correspondence and service regarding this filing should be sent to the following

        B. Documents Submitted with This Filing

        In accordance with the requirements of Order No. 714 22 and the Commission’s eTariff
regulations, LG&E is submitting an eTariff XML filing package consisting of the following
materials:

           This Transmittal Letter;
           Attachment A: A redlined-tariff version showing the changes to the Attachment O
            formula rate, as described herein, for filing in eLibrary;
           Attachment B: A clean-tariff version of LG&E/KU’s revised Attachment O for filing
            in eTariff and eLibrary;
           Attachment C: Testimony and exhibits of John J. Spanos;
           Attachment D: Depreciation Rate Change Impact; and
           Attachment E: Detail of Attachment O Revisions.

        C. Request for Waiver

        This filing substantially complies with the requirements of Part 35 of the Commission’s
regulations applicable to filings of this kind. To the extent necessary, LG&E respectfully
requests waiver of any applicable requirement of Part 35 of the Commission’s regulations which
is found not to be completely satisfied by this filing.
 V.     Conclusion

        WHEREFORE, for the foregoing reasons, LG&E respectfully requests that the
Commission issue an order by December 29, 2026, accepting the Attachment O Revisions to be
effective as requested herein, and grant any necessary waivers.

Attachment C
                            BEFORE THE
                    UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
             FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION


Louisville Gas and Electric Company and   )       Docket Nos.   ER27-____-000
Kentucky Utilities Company




                      PREPARED DIRECT TESTIMONY

                                      OF

                               JOHN J. SPANOS

                               ON BEHALF OF

LOUISVILLE GAS AND ELECTRIC COMPANY AND KENTUCKY UTILITIES
                         COMPANY




                               October 28, 2026
                                                TABLE OF CONTENTS

                                                                                                                         PAGE

III. CONCLUSION ................................................................................................................ 23
                       I.      INTRODUCTION AND PURPOSE

 1   Q.   PLEASE STATE YOUR NAME AND ADDRESS.

 2   A.   My name is John J. Spanos.        My business address is 300 Sterling Parkway,

 3        Mechanicsburg, Pennsylvania.

 4   Q.   ARE YOU ASSOCIATED WITH ANY FIRM?

 5   A.   Yes.   I am associated with the firm of Gannett Fleming Valuation and Rate

 6        Consultants, LLC (“Gannett Fleming”), a subsidiary of GFT Infrastructure, Inc.

 7   Q.   HOW LONG HAVE YOU BEEN ASSOCIATED WITH GANNETT

 8        FLEMING?

 9   A.   I have been associated with the firm since June, 1986.

10   Q.   WHAT IS YOUR POSITION WITH THE FIRM?

11   A.   I am President.

12   Q.   WHAT IS YOUR EDUCATIONAL BACKGROUND?

13   A.   I have Bachelor of Science degrees in Industrial Management and Mathematics from

14        Carnegie-Mellon University and a Master of Business Administration from York

15        College of Pennsylvania.

16   Q.   DO YOU BELONG TO ANY PROFESSIONAL SOCIETIES?

17   A.   Yes.   I am a member and a past President of the Society of Depreciation

18        Professionals. I am also a member of the American Gas Association/Edison Electric

19        Institute Industry Accounting Committee.

20




                                     JOHN J. SPANOS DIRECT
                                               2
  1   Q.   ON WHOSE BEHALF ARE YOU TESTIFYING IN THE CASE?

 2   A.   I am testifying on behalf of Louisville Gas and Electric Company (“LG&E”) and

 3        Kentucky Utilities Company (“KU”) (each a “Company,” and together, the

 4        “Companies”).

 5   Q.   PLEASE      OUTLINE        YOUR      EXPERIENCE         IN    THE     FIELD       OF

 6        DEPRECIATION.

 7   A.   I have over 40 years of depreciation experience, which includes giving expert

 8        testimony in in more than 550 cases before 47 regulatory commissions, including this

 9        Commission. The cases include depreciation studies in the electric, gas, water,

10        wastewater and pipeline industries. In addition to the cases that I have submitted

11        testimony, I have supervised over 900 other depreciation or valuation projects.

12               Please refer to Appendix A for my qualifications statement, which includes

13        further information with respect to my work history, case experience, and leadership

14        in the Society of Depreciation Professionals.

15   Q.   WHAT      IS    THE     PURPOSE       OF        YOUR   TESTIMONY         IN   THIS

16        PROCEEDING?

17   A.   My testimony will support and explain the combined depreciation study conducted

18        under my direction and supervision for LG&E and KU, in advance of the Companies’

19        planned merger. This study is attached hereto as Exhibit JJS-1. The study represents

20        all electric and common plant.

21




                                    JOHN J. SPANOS DIRECT
                                                3
                                II.    DEPRECIATION STUDY

 1   Q.   PLEASE DEFINE THE CONCEPT OF DEPRECIATION.

 2   A.   Depreciation refers to the loss in service value not restored by current maintenance,

 3        incurred in connection with the consumption or prospective retirement of utility plant

 4        in the course of service from causes which are known to be in current operation,

 5        against which the company is not protected by insurance. Among the causes to be

 6        given consideration are wear and tear, decay, action of the elements, inadequacy,

 7        obsolescence, changes in the art, changes in demand and the requirements of public

 8        authorities.

 9   Q.   DID YOU PREPARE THE COMBINED DEPRECIATION STUDY FILED BY

10        LG&E AND KU IN THIS PROCEEDING?

11   A.   Yes. I prepared the combined depreciation study submitted by LG&E and KU with

12        their filing in this proceeding, in anticipation of their forthcoming merger. My report

13        is entitled: “2025 Depreciation Study - Calculated Annual Depreciation Accruals

14        Related to Electric and Common Plant as of December 31, 2025.” The report sets

15        forth the results of my depreciation study for the merged Companies.

16   Q.   IN PREPARING THE DEPRECIATION STUDY, DID YOU FOLLOW

17        GENERALLY          ACCEPTED          PRACTICES          IN    THE      FIELD       OF

18        DEPRECIATION VALUATION?

19   A.   Yes.

20




                                     JOHN J. SPANOS DIRECT
                                                 4
  1   Q.   ARE THE METHODS AND PROCEDURES OF THIS DEPRECIATION

 2        STUDY CONSISTENT WITH PAST PRACTICES?

 3   A.   Yes. The methods and procedures of this study are the same as those utilized in past

 4        studies of each Company as well as others before this Commission. The depreciation

 5        rates recommended in my study are determined based on the average service life

 6        procedure and the remaining life method.

 7   Q.   ARE THE UNDERLYING LIFE AND NET SALVAGE PARAMETERS AND

 8        RESULTING DEPRECIATION ISSUES IN THIS STUDY CONSISTENT

 9        WITH INDUSTRY TRENDS?

10   A.   Yes. The life and net salvage parameters for the merged Companies have changed

11        consistently with others in the industry as well as the major changes to the production

12        asset mix which includes some shorter and longer remaining lives for steam facilities

13        and longer remaining lives for combustion turbines.

14   Q.   WHAT WAS THE PURPOSE OF YOUR DEPRECIATION STUDY?

15   A.   The purpose of the Depreciation Study was to estimate the annual depreciation

16        accruals related to electric and common plant in service for ratemaking purposes and

17        determine appropriate average service lives and net salvage percents for each plant

18        account for the merged Companies. Additionally, this study incorporates the transfer

19        of assets to the new FERC Order 898 accounts.

20   Q.   PLEASE DESCRIBE THE CONTENTS OF YOUR REPORT.

21   A.   The Depreciation Study is presented in nine parts. Part I, Introduction, presents the

22        scope and basis for the depreciation study. Part II, Estimation of Survivor Curves,

23        includes descriptions of the methodology of estimating survivor curves. Parts III and


                                    JOHN J. SPANOS DIRECT
                                                5
  1        IV set forth the analysis for determining life and net salvage estimates. Part V,

 2        Calculation of Annual and Accrued Depreciation, includes the concepts of

 3        depreciation using the remaining life.       Part VI, Results of Study, presents a

 4        description of the results of my analysis and a summary of the depreciation

 5        calculations. Parts VII, VIII and IX include graphs and tables that relate to the service

 6        life and net salvage analyses, and the detailed depreciation calculations by account.

 7               Tables 1 and 2 on pages VI-4 through VI-15 of Exhibit JJS-1 present the

 8        estimated survivor curve, the net salvage percent, the original cost as of December

 9        31, 2025, the book depreciation reserve, and the calculated annual depreciation

10        accrual and rate for each account or subaccount. The section beginning on page VII-

11        2 presents the results of the retirement rate analyses prepared as the historical bases

12        for the service life estimates. The section beginning on page VIII-2 presents the

13        results of the net salvage analysis. The section beginning on page IX-2 presents the

14        depreciation calculations related to surviving original cost as of December 31, 2025.

15   Q.   PLEASE EXPLAIN HOW YOU PERFORMED YOUR DEPRECIATION

16        STUDY.

17   A.   I used the straight line remaining life method of depreciation, with the average service

18        life procedure. The annual depreciation is based on a method of depreciation

19        accounting that seeks to distribute the unrecovered cost of fixed capital assets over

20        the estimated remaining useful life of each unit, or group of assets, in a systematic

21        and reasonable manner.

22




                                     JOHN J. SPANOS DIRECT
                                                 6
  1   Q.   HOW      DID     YOU      DETERMINE          THE     RECOMMENDED              ANNUAL

 2        DEPRECIATION ACCRUAL RATES?

 3   A.   I did this in two phases. In the first phase, I estimated the service life and net salvage

 4        characteristics for each depreciable group, that is, each plant account or subaccount

 5        identified as having similar characteristics. In the second phase, I calculated the

 6        composite remaining lives and annual depreciation accrual rates based on the service

 7        life and net salvage estimates determined in the first phase.

 8                For Electric General Plant Accounts 391.10, 393.00, 394.00, 397.10, 397.11.

 9        397.20, 397.21, 397.22, 397.23, 397.30, 397.31 and 398.00; and Common General

10        Plant Accounts 391.10, 391.20, 391.40, 393.00, 394.00, 397.10, 397.11, 397.12,

11        397.21, 397.22, 397.23, 397.24, 397.26, 397.30, 397.31, 397.33 and 398.00, I used

12        the straight line remaining life method of amortization. Annual amortization also

13        applies to new FERC Order 898 accounts that were transferred from existing general

14        amortized accounts. The annual amortization is based on amortization accounting

15        that distributes the unrecovered cost of fixed capital assets over the remaining

16        amortization period selected for each account and vintage.

17   Q.   PLEASE DESCRIBE THE FIRST PHASE OF THE DEPRECIATION

18        STUDY, IN WHICH YOU ESTIMATED THE SERVICE LIFE AND NET

19        SALVAGE CHARACTERISTICS FOR EACH DEPRECIABLE GROUP?

20   A.   The service life and net salvage studies consisted of compiling historical data from

21        records related to the original LG&E’s and KU’s plant; analyzing these data as

22        merged Companies to obtain historical trends of survivor characteristics; obtaining

23        supplementary information from management and operating personnel concerning


                                     JOHN J. SPANOS DIRECT
                                                  7
  1        practices and plans related to plant operations; and interpreting the data and the

 2        estimates used by other electric utilities to form judgments of average service life and

 3        net salvage characteristics.

 4   Q.   WHAT HISTORICAL DATA DID YOU ANALYZE FOR THE PURPOSE OF

 5        ESTIMATING SERVICE LIFE CHARACTERISTICS?

 6   A.   Generally, I analyzed the combined Companies’ accounting entries that record plant

 7        transactions during the period 1900 through 2025 for electric plant and 1910 through

 8        2025 for common plant. The transactions included additions, retirements, transfers,

 9        sales and the related balances.

10   Q.   WHAT METHOD DID YOU USE TO ANALYZE THESE SERVICE LIFE

11        DATA?

12   A.   I used the retirement rate method. This is the most appropriate method when

13        retirement data covering a long period of time is available because this method

14        determines the average rates of retirement actually experienced by the combined

15        Companies during the period of time covered by the depreciation study.

16   Q.   PLEASE DESCRIBE HOW YOU USED THE RETIREMENT RATE

17        METHOD TO ANALYZE BOTH COMPANIES’ SERVICE LIFE DATA.

18   A.   I applied the retirement rate analysis to each different group of property in each study.

19        For each property group, I used the retirement rate data to form a life table which,

20        when plotted, shows an original survivor curve for that property group. Each original

21        survivor curve represents the average survivor pattern experienced by the several

22        vintage groups during the experience band studied. The survivor patterns do not

23        necessarily describe the life characteristics of the property group; therefore,


                                     JOHN J. SPANOS DIRECT
                                                 8
  1        interpretation of the original survivor curves is required in order to use them as valid

 2        considerations in estimating service life. The Iowa type survivor curves were used

 3        to perform these interpretations.

 4   Q.   WHAT IS AN “IOWA-TYPE SURVIVOR CURVE” AND HOW DID YOU

 5        USE     SUCH       CURVES           TO   ESTIMATE        THE      SERVICE        LIFE

 6        CHARACTERISTICS FOR EACH PROPERTY GROUP?

 7   A.   Iowa type curves are a widely-used group of survivor curves that contain the range

 8        of survivor characteristics usually experienced by utilities and other industrial

 9        companies. A survivor curve is a graphical depiction of the amount of property

10        existing at each age throughout the life of an asset class. The Iowa curves were

11        developed at the Iowa State College Engineering Experiment Station through an

12        extensive process of observing and classifying the ages at which various types of

13        property used by utilities and other industrial companies had been retired.

14               Iowa type curves are used to smooth and extrapolate original survivor curves

15        determined by the retirement rate method. The Iowa curves and truncated Iowa

16        curves were used in this study to describe the forecasted rates of retirement based on

17        the observed rates of retirement and the outlook for future retirements.

18               The estimated survivor curve designations for each depreciable property

19        group indicate the average service life, the family within the Iowa curve system to

20        which the property group belongs, and the relative height of the mode. For example,

21        the Iowa 47-R1 indicates an average service life of forty-seven years; a right-moded,

22        or R, type curve (the mode occurs after average life for right-moded curves); and a

23        low height, 1, for the mode (possible modes for R type curves range from 0.5 to 5).


                                    JOHN J. SPANOS DIRECT
                                                   9
  1   Q.   WHAT APPROACH DID YOU USE TO ESTIMATE THE LIVES OF

 2        SIGNIFICANT FACILITIES STRUCTURES SUCH AS PRODUCTION

 3        PLANTS?

 4   A.   I used the life span technique to estimate the lives of significant facilities for which

 5        concurrent retirement of the entire facility is anticipated. In this technique, the

 6        survivor characteristics of such facilities are described by the use of interim survivor

 7        curves and estimated probable retirement dates.

 8                The interim survivor curves describe the rate of retirement related to the

 9        replacement of elements of the facility, such as, for a building, the retirements of

10        plumbing, heating, doors, windows, roofs, etc., that occurs during the life of the

11        facility. The probable retirement date provides the rate of final retirement for each

12        year of installation for the facility by truncating the interim survivor curve for each

13        installation year at its attained age at the date of probable retirement. The use of

14        interim survivor curves truncated at the date of probable retirement provides a

15        consistent method for estimating the lives of the several years of installation for a

16        particular facility inasmuch as a single concurrent retirement for all years of

17        installation will occur when it is retired.

18   Q.   HAS GANNETT FLEMING USED THIS APPROACH IN OTHER

19        PROCEEDINGS?

20   A.   Yes, we have used the life span technique in performing depreciation studies

21        presented to and accepted by many public utility commissions across the United

22        States and Canada, including the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (“FERC”).




                                     JOHN J. SPANOS DIRECT
                                                  10
  1        The life span technique is currently being utilized by the Companies in the same

 2        manner recommended in this case for developing depreciation rates.

 3   Q.   WHAT ARE THE BASES FOR THE PROBABLE RETIREMENT YEARS

 4        THAT YOU HAVE ESTIMATED FOR EACH FACILITY?

 5   A.   The bases for the probable retirement years are life spans for each facility that are

 6        based on informed judgment, and incorporate consideration of the age, use, size,

 7        nature of construction, management outlook and typical life spans experienced and

 8        used by other electric utilities for similar facilities. Most of the life spans result in

 9        probable retirement years that are many years in the future.           As a result, the

10        retirements of these facilities are not yet subject to specific management plans. Such

11        plans would be premature. At the appropriate time, studies of the economics of

12        rehabilitation and continued use or retirement of the structure will be performed and

13        the results incorporated into the estimation of the facility’s life span. Per discussions

14        with the Companies’ personnel in prior studies and this study, the planning and

15        analysis which contributed to the determination of the probable retirement date of

16        each unit in the generation fleet are consistent with how each probable retirement

17        date has been established and currently in affect.

18   Q.   ARE THE LIFE SPANS REASONABLE?

19   A.   Yes. The most common range of life spans for steam production facilities had been

20        55 to 65 years; however, in recent years, originally proposed life spans have changed

21        due to unit efficiencies and environmental regulations. The industry average of

22        similar units in recent years has been 46 years. For combustion turbines, the most

23        common period for life spans has been 40 years. The existing solar facilities have a


                                     JOHN J. SPANOS DIRECT
                                                 11
  1        life span of 25 years, which is consistent with the most recent installations. However,

 2        future solar facilities with some newer design will have a life span of 30 years. The

 3        Brown Wind facility has a 25 year life span from the time the asset started generating.

 4   Q.   DO TRANSMISSION ASSETS HAVE A LIFE SPAN COMPONENT?

 5   A.   No. All the transmission assets are considered mass property and do not have one

 6        concurrent date of retirement so there is no life span component in the overall life

 7        characteristics.

 8   Q.   ARE THE FACTORS CONSIDERED IN YOUR ESTIMATES OF SERVICE

 9        LIFE AND NET SALVAGE PERCENTS PRESENTED IN EXHIBIT JJS-1?

10   A.   Yes. A discussion of the factors considered in the estimation of service lives and net

11        salvage percents are presented in Part III and Part IV of the exhibit.

12   Q.   HAVE YOU PHYSICALLY OBSERVED THE COMPANIES’ PLANT AND

13        EQUIPMENT AS PART OF YOUR DEPRECIATION STUDY?

14   A.   Yes. I made a field review of the Companies’ property during October 2024 to

15        observe representative portions of plant. I have also conducted field reviews of the

16        Companies’ property as part of past studies during April and May 2007, October

17        2011, October 2015 and October 2019. Field reviews are commonly taken every 4

18        to 5 years in order to identify change in asset condition. Field reviews are conducted

19        to become familiar with a company’s operations and obtain an understanding of the

20        function of the plant and information with respect to the reasons for past retirements

21        and the expected future causes of retirements. This knowledge as well as information

22        from other discussions with management was incorporated in the interpretation and

23        extrapolation of the statistical analyses.


                                     JOHN J. SPANOS DIRECT
                                                 12
  1   Q.   PLEASE       DESCRIBE        HOW       YOU      ESTIMATED          NET      SALVAGE

 2        PERCENTAGES.

 3   A.   I estimated the net salvage percentages by incorporating the historical data for the

 4        period 1972 through 2025 and considered estimates for other electric companies.

 5   Q.   WOULD YOU PLEASE EXPLAIN THE CONCEPT OF “NET SALVAGE”?

 6   A.   Net salvage is a component of the service value of capital assets that is recovered

 7        through depreciation rates. The service value of an asset is its original cost less its

 8        net salvage. Net salvage is the gross salvage value received for the asset upon

 9        retirement less the cost to retire the asset. When the cost to retire exceeds the gross

10        salvage value, the result is negative net salvage.

11               Inasmuch as depreciation expense is the loss in service value of an asset

12        during a defined period, e.g., one year, it must include a ratable portion of both the

13        original cost and the net salvage. That is, the net salvage related to an asset should

14        be incorporated in the cost of service during the same period as its original cost so

15        that customers receiving service from the asset pay rates that include a portion of

16        both elements of the asset’s service value, the original cost, and the net salvage value.

17               For example, the full recovery of the service value of a $5,000 line

18        transformer will include not only the $5,000 of original cost, but also, on average,

19        $300 to remove the line transformer at the end of its life and $50 in salvage value. In

20        this example, the net salvage component is negative $250 ($50 - $300), and the net

21        salvage percent is negative 5% (($50 - $300)/$5,000).

22




                                     JOHN J. SPANOS DIRECT
                                                 13
  1   Q.   PLEASE       DESCRIBE           HOW    YOU      ESTIMATED          NET      SALVAGE

 2        PERCENTAGES.

 3   A.   The net salvage percentages estimated in the Depreciation Study were based on

 4        informed judgment that incorporated factors such as the statistical analyses of

 5        historical net salvage data; information provided to me by the Companies’ operating

 6        personnel, general knowledge and experience of the industry practices; and trends in

 7        the industry in general. The statistical net salvage analyses incorporates the actual

 8        historical data for the period 1972 through 2025, and considers the cost of removal

 9        and gross salvage ratios to the associated retirements during the same periods. Trends

10        of these data are also measured based on three-year moving averages and the most

11        recent five-year indications.

10   A.   The average service life procedure defines the group or account for which the

11        remaining life annual accrual is determined. Under this procedure, the annual accrual

12        rate is determined for the entire group or account based on its average remaining life

13        and the rate is then applied to the surviving balance of the group’s cost. The average

14        remaining life of the group is calculated by first dividing the future book accruals

17        derived from the area under the survivor curve between the attained age of the vintage

18        and the maximum age. The sum of the future book accruals is then divided by the

19        sum of the annual accruals to determine the average remaining life of the entire group

 2   A.   Amortization accounting is used for accounts with a large number of units, but small

 3        asset values. In amortization accounting, units of property are capitalized in the same

 4        manner as they are in depreciation accounting. However, depreciation accounting is

 5        difficult for these assets because periodic inventories are required to properly reflect

 6        plant in service. Consequently, retirements are recorded when a vintage is fully

 7        amortized rather than as the units are removed from service. That is, there is no

 8        dispersion of retirement. All units are retired when the age of the vintage reaches the

 9        amortization period. Each plant account or group of assets is assigned a fixed period

10        which represents an anticipated life during which the asset will render service. For

11        example, in amortization accounting, assets that have a 25-year amortization period

12        will be fully recovered after 25 years of service and taken off the books, but not

13        necessarily removed from service. In contrast, assets that are taken out of service

14        before 25 years remain on the books until the amortization period for that vintage has

15        expired.

BASIS OF THE STUDY

Depreciation

        Depreciation, in public utility regulation, is the loss in service value not restored

by current maintenance, incurred in connection with the consumption or prospective

retirement of utility plant in the course of service from causes which are known to be

in current operation and against which the utility is not protected by insurance.

Among causes to be given consideration are wear and tear, deterioration, action of

the elements, inadequacy, obsolescence, changes in the art, changes in demand, and

the requirements of public authorities.

       Depreciation, as used in accounting, is a method of distributing fixed capital costs,

less net salvage, over a period of time by allocating annual amounts to expense.

Each annual amount of such depreciation expense is part of that year's total cost of

providing electric utility service.   Normally, the period of time over which the fixed

capital cost is allocated to the cost of service is equal to the period of time over which

an item renders service, that is, the item's service life. The most prevalent method

of allocation is to distribute an equal amount of cost to each year of service life.

This method is known as the straight line method of depreciation.

                     PART II. ESTIMATION OF SURVIVOR CURVES

       The calculation of annual depreciation based on the straight line method requires

the estimation of survivor curves and the selection of group depreciation procedures. The

estimation of survivor curves is discussed below, and the development of net salvage is

discussed in later sections of this report.


SURVIVOR CURVES

       The use of an average service life for a property group implies that the various

units in the group have different lives.      Thus, the average life may be obtained by

determining the separate lives of each of the units or by constructing a survivor curve by

plotting the number of units which survive at successive ages.

       The survivor curve graphically depicts the amount of property existing at each age

throughout the life of an original group. From the survivor curve, the average life of the

group, the remaining life expectancy, the probable life, and the frequency curve can be

calculated. In Figure 1, a typical smooth survivor curve and the derived curves are

illustrated. The average life is obtained by calculating the area under the survivor curve,

from age zero to the maximum age, and dividing this area by the ordinate at age zero.

The remaining life expectancy at any age can be calculated by obtaining the area under

the curve, from the observation age to the maximum age, and dividing this area by the

percent surviving at the observation age. For example, in Figure 1, the remaining life at

age 30 is equal to the crosshatched area under the survivor curve divided by 29.5 percent

surviving at age 30. The probable life at any age is developed by adding the age and

remaining life. If the probable life of the property is calculated for each year of age, the

probable life curve shown in the chart can be developed. The frequency curve presents

the number of units retired in each age interval. It is derived by obtaining the differences

between the amount of property surviving at the beginning and at the end of each interval.

Iowa Type Curves
       The range of survivor characteristics usually experienced by utility and industrial
properties is encompassed by a system of generalized survivor curves known as the Iowa

type curves. There are four families in the Iowa system, labeled in accordance with the
location of the modes of the retirements (or the portion of the frequency curve with the
highest level of retirements) in relationship to the average life and the relative height of

the modes. The left moded curves, presented in Figure 2, are those in which the greatest
frequency of retirement occurs to the left of, or prior to, average service life. The
symmetrical moded curves, presented in Figure 3, are those in which the greatest

frequency of retirement occurs at average service life. The right moded curves, presented
in Figure 4, are those in which the greatest frequency occurs to the right of, or after,
average service life. The origin moded curves, presented in Figure 5, are those in which

the greatest frequency of retirement occurs at the origin, or immediately after age zero.
The letter designation of each family of curves (L, S, R or O) represents the location of
the mode of the associated frequency curve with respect to the average service life. The

numbers represent the relative heights of the modes of the frequency curves within each
family. A higher number designates a higher mode curve.
       The Iowa curves were developed at the Iowa State College Engineering

Experiment Station through an extensive process of observation and classification of the
ages at which industrial property had been retired. A report of the study which resulted
in the classification of property survivor characteristics into 18 type curves, which

constitute three of the four families, was published in 1935 in the form of the Experiment
Station’s Bulletin 125.

Retirement Rate Method of Analysis
       The retirement rate method is an actuarial method of deriving survivor curves using
the average rates at which property of each age group is retired. The method relates to

property groups for which aged accounting experience is available and is the method
used to develop the original stub survivor curves in this study. The method (also known
as the annual rate method) is illustrated through the use of an example in the following

text and is also explained in several publications including "Statistical Analyses of
Industrial Property Retirements," 2 "Engineering Valuation and Depreciation," 3 and
"Depreciation Systems." 4

       The average rate of retirement used in the calculation of the percent surviving for
the survivor curve (life table) requires two sets of data: first, the property retired during a
period of observation, identified by the property's age at retirement; and second, the

property exposed to retirement at the beginning of the age intervals during the same
period. The period of observation is referred to as the experience band. The band of
years which represent the installation dates of the property exposed to retirement during

the experience band is referred to as the placement band. An example of the calculations
used in the development of a life table follows. The example includes schedules of annual
aged property transactions, a schedule of plant exposed to retirement, a life table and

Original Life Table
       The original life table, illustrated in Schedule 4 on page II-16, is developed from

the totals shown on the schedules of retirements and exposures, Schedules 1 and 3,
respectively. The exposures at the beginning of the age interval are obtained from the
corresponding age interval of the exposure schedule, and the retirements during the age

interval are obtained from the corresponding age interval of the retirement schedule. The
retirement ratio is the result of dividing the retirements during the age interval by the
exposures at the beginning of the age interval. The percent surviving at the beginning of

each age interval is derived from survivor ratios, each of which equals one minus the
retirement ratio. The percent surviving is developed by starting with 100% at age zero
and successively multiplying the percent surviving at the beginning of each interval by the

survivor ratio, i.e., one minus the retirement ratio for that age interval. The calculations
necessary to determine the percent surviving at age 5½ are as follows:

       Retirement Ratio                    = 143,000 ÷ 3,789,000 = 0.0377
       Survivor Ratio                      =     1.000 -    0.0377 = 0.9623
       Percent surviving at age 5½         =    (88.15) x (0.9623) = 84.83

Smoothing the Original Survivor Curve

       The smoothing of the original survivor curve eliminates any irregularities and

serves as the basis for the preliminary extrapolation to zero percent surviving of the

original stub curve. Even if the original survivor curve is complete from 100% to zero

percent, it is desirable to eliminate any irregularities, as there is still an extrapolation for

the vintages which have not yet lived to the age at which the curve reaches zero percent.

to eliminate irregularities in the original curve.

GROUP DEPRECIATION PROCEDURES

       A group procedure for depreciation is appropriate when considering more than a

single item of property. Normally the items within a group do not have identical service

lives, but have lives that are dispersed over a range of time. There are two primary

group procedures, namely, average service life and equal life group. In the average

service life procedure, the rate of annual depreciation is based on the average life

or average remaining life of the group, and this rate is applied to the surviving balances

of the group's cost. A characteristic of this procedure is that the cost of plant retired prior

to average life is not fully recouped at the time of retirement, whereas the cost of plant

retired subsequent to average life is more than fully recouped. Over the entire life cycle,

the portion of cost not recouped prior to average life is balanced by the cost recouped

subsequent to average life.
